course.title: Dari, Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: Afghan Dari Persian from absolute beginner through fluent, everyday command -- real sentences, grammar, and conversational practice
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real sentences from lesson one, built the same way as this app's other courses.

questions.title: Asking Questions
questions.explanation: Dari question words stay right where the answer would go, rather than moving to the front the way English does. "شما کجا هستید؟" is literally "You where are?" -- کجا (kojā, where) simply sits in the spot the place-answer would fill. The same is true for چی (chi, what), کی (kay, when), چرا (cherā, why), and چند (chand, how many).
questions.fact: چند (chand) does double duty: alone before a noun it means "how many/how much" (چند کتاب؟ "how many books?"), but with -م attached it becomes چندم ("which number in order") for asking someone's rank or position.

dialogue.en: Where do you work?

dialogue.native: من در یک دوکان کار می‌کنم.
dialogue.en: I work in a shop.

dialogue.native: چند سال است که آنجا کار می‌کنید؟
dialogue.en: How many years have you worked there?

prepositions-location.title: Saying Where Something Is
prepositions-location.explanation: Location words like در (in), نزدیک (near), دور (far from), زیر (under), and روی (on) come directly before the place they describe, just like English "in," "near," "under." کتاب روی میز است is "the book is on the table."
prepositions-location.fact: روی literally means "face" as a noun (as in چهره/روی, "face") -- "on top of" grew out of the image of something resting face-up on a surface.

dialogue.en: Where is my book?
It's on the table.

dialogue.native: خانه شما نزدیک است یا دور؟
dialogue.en: Is your house near or far?

adjectives-order.title: Describing Things: Adjective After the Noun
adjectives-order.explanation: In Dari, the describing word comes AFTER the noun, joined by an unwritten -e/-ye sound (the ezafe): خانهٔ بزرگ (khāna-ye bozorg) is literally "house-of big," meaning "a/the big house." This is the opposite order from English "big house." The ezafe is not usually written, but it is always pronounced.
adjectives-order.fact: The same ezafe -e/-ye links a noun to its owner too, which you already saw in نام شما (nām-e shomā, "your name") — one small grammatical glue connects both descriptions and possession.

dialogue.en: This is a big house.

dialogue.native: موتر شما نو است یا کهنه؟
dialogue.en: Is your car new or old?
My car is new.

present-tense.title: Talking About Now: The Present Tense
present-tense.explanation: Most Dari verbs build their present tense with می in front of a present stem, then a personal ending: می‌روم (I go), می‌روی (you go), می‌رود (he/she goes), می‌رویم (we go), می‌روید (you all go), می‌روند (they go). The tricky part is that the present stem often looks nothing like the dictionary (infinitive) form -- رفتن (raftan, "to go") has the stem رو (raw), and دیدن (didan, "to see") has the stem بین (bin). These stems have to be learned one at a time, the same way English learners must simply learn that "go" becomes "went."
present-tense.fact: Because the personal ending already shows who is doing the action, Dari sentences very often drop the separate pronoun altogether -- می‌روم alone already means "I go," no من needed.

dialogue.native: شما هر روز به مکتب می‌روید؟
dialogue.en: Do you go to school every day?
Yes, I go every day.
I also drink tea in the morning.

greetings-copula.title: Greeting Someone and Saying "I am..."
greetings-copula.explanation: Dari's "to be" verb (بودن) comes AFTER the word it describes, unlike English "I am good" -> "من خوب هستم" is literally "I good am." Each person has its own ending: هستم (I am), هستی (you are, one friend), است (he/she/it is), هستیم (we are), هستید (you are, formal or more than one person), هستند (they are). This copula is often shortened to -am/-i/-ast/-im/-id/-and in fast speech, but the full forms here are always correct and are what you will see written.
greetings-copula.fact: شما (shomā) works as both a polite "you" for one person and the plain "you" for a group -- Dari does not force a separate plural pronoun the way English needs "you all."

dialogue.en: Hello, how are you?

dialogue.native: من خوب هستم، تشکر. تو چطور هستی؟
dialogue.en: I am good, thank you. How are you?
I am also good.

past-tense.title: Talking About the Past
past-tense.explanation: The simple past is much more regular than the present: for almost every verb, the past stem is just the infinitive with the final ن removed. رفتن (raftan, "to go") -> رفت (raft, "went"); خوردن (khordan, "to eat") -> خورد (khord, "ate"). Personal endings attach directly, and the "he/she/it" form has NO ending at all -- the bare past stem alone already means "he/she/it did."
past-tense.fact: Because the present tense stems are so irregular but the past stems are so regular, many Dari textbooks actually teach the past tense before the present -- it is the easier one to predict.

dialogue.en: Where did you go yesterday?

dialogue.native: من به بازار رفتم و میوه خریدم.
dialogue.en: I went to the market and bought fruit.
Was it good?

plurals-comparatives.title: More Than One, and Comparing Things
plurals-comparatives.explanation: To make almost any Dari noun plural, add ها to the end: کتاب (book) -> کتاب‌ها (books). To compare two things, add تر to an adjective: بزرگ (big) -> بزرگ‌تر (bigger). Adding ترین instead makes the superlative: بزرگ‌ترین (the biggest).
plurals-comparatives.fact: بهتر ("better") and بدتر ("worse") are irregular comparatives, built from به/خوب (good) and بد (bad) -- the same kind of exception English has with "good -> better," not "gooder."

dialogue.en: Are these books yours?

dialogue.native: بلی، این کتاب از آن کتاب بهتر است.
dialogue.en: Yes, this book is better than that book.
Which book is the biggest?

reported-speech.title: Telling What Someone Said
reported-speech.explanation: To report what someone said, Dari uses گفت که ("said that") followed by the reported sentence, often keeping the same tense the speaker actually used (unlike English, which usually shifts tense back): او گفت که فردا می‌آید ("He/she said that he/she is coming tomorrow") keeps می‌آید rather than shifting to a past form.
reported-speech.fact: که (ke) is one of the hardest-working words in Dari -- the very same که links relative clauses ("the book that..."), reported speech ("said that..."), and reasons ("because..."), with context telling them apart.

dialogue.en: He/she said that he/she is not coming tomorrow.
Why? I asked.
He/she said that he/she has a lot of work.

conditionals.title: If... Then...: Real Conditions
conditionals.explanation: اگر (agar, "if") introduces the condition, and the result follows, often with a comma between them: اگر باران ببارد، ما در خانه می‌مانیم ("If it rains, we will stay home"). For a condition that's still open/possible, the subjunctive (بـ + present stem) is common in the if-clause; for something already decided or habitual, the plain present tense works too.
conditionals.fact: اگر can also mean "since/given that" in some contexts, not only hypothetical "if" -- context usually makes the meaning clear.

dialogue.native: اگر وقت داشته باشید، به خانه ما بیایید.
dialogue.en: If you have time, come to our house.

dialogue.native: اگر امکان داشته باشد، حتماً می‌آیم.
dialogue.en: If it's possible, I will definitely come.
Good, we'll be waiting for you.

present-perfect.title: Something That Has Happened: The Present Perfect
present-perfect.explanation: To say something has happened (with relevance to now), Dari uses the past participle -- the past stem plus ه -- followed by a shortened form of "to be": رفته‌ام (I have gone), رفته‌ای (you have gone), رفته است (he/she has gone), رفته‌ایم (we have gone), رفته‌اید (you all have gone), رفته‌اند (they have gone). This is different from the simple past (رفتم, "I went") -- the present perfect points at a result that still matters right now.
present-perfect.fact: In fast, everyday speech, رفته است often shortens further to رفته، with the است dropped or merged -- but the full written form is always safe and correct.

dialogue.en: Have you read this book?

dialogue.native: بلی، من این کتاب را خوانده‌ام.
dialogue.en: Yes, I have read this book.
How was it?

passive-voice.title: The Passive Voice
passive-voice.explanation: Dari builds the passive by pairing a past participle with the verb شدن ("to become"): نوشته شد ("it was written"), ساخته می‌شود ("it is being built"), گفته شده است ("it has been said"). The doer of the action is often left out entirely, exactly as in English "the book was written" (by whom, unstated).
passive-voice.fact: Because شدن also means plain "to become," a sentence like او معلم شد can mean either "he/she became a teacher" (active) -- passive meaning only shows up when a real past participle comes right before شدن.

dialogue.native: این کتاب در سال گذشته نوشته شد.
dialogue.en: This book was written last year.
By whom was it written?
Its writer is famous.

complex-clauses.title: Combining Ideas Into One Sentence
complex-clauses.explanation: At this level, sentences often stack multiple clauses together using که (that/which), اگرچه (although), and other connectors already learned -- the individual pieces are all familiar, but B2 fluency means combining them naturally into longer, more precise thoughts, the way an educated native speaker actually talks about complex topics.
complex-clauses.fact: Formal written Dari (in newspapers, academic writing, official documents) tends to prefer these long, layered sentences, while everyday spoken Dari breaks the same ideas into several shorter sentences -- recognizing both styles is part of real fluency.

dialogue.native: نظریه‌ای که او مطرح کرد، جالب بود اما همه با آن موافق نبودند.
dialogue.en: The theory that he/she proposed was interesting, but not everyone agreed with it.
Why were some opposed?

dialogue.native: زیرا فکر می‌کردند که دلیل کافی وجود ندارد.
dialogue.en: Because they thought there wasn't enough evidence.

nuanced-register.title: Formal Register and Idiomatic Expression
nuanced-register.explanation: At this level, fluent Dari draws on proverbs (مثل‌ها), set idiomatic expressions, and a more elevated vocabulary choice to make a point land with more weight -- the same way an English speaker might reach for "actions speak louder than words" instead of just saying "do things, don't just talk." Recognizing and using these expressions naturally is a marker of near-native fluency.
nuanced-register.fact: Many Dari proverbs share roots with proverbs across the wider Persian-speaking world (Iran, Tajikistan) and sometimes with Pashto proverbs too, reflecting centuries of shared and neighboring culture in the region.

dialogue.native: می‌گویند که صبر تلخ است اما میوه‌اش شیرین است.
dialogue.en: They say that patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet.
What does this proverb mean?

dialogue.native: یعنی اگر صبر کنیم، در نهایت نتیجه خوبی می‌گیریم.
dialogue.en: It means if we are patient, in the end we get a good result.

advanced-argument.title: Building a Sustained Argument
advanced-argument.explanation: At C1, the goal is no longer any single grammar point -- it's sustaining a real argument across several connected sentences the way an essay, a lecture, or a serious conversation would, moving from a claim, through evidence and counter-evidence, to a considered conclusion, all in natural, idiomatic Dari.
advanced-argument.fact: Formal C1-level Dari prose often favors nominalized, abstract phrasing ("the growth of awareness" rather than "people became more aware") -- a stylistic register shift, not a new grammar rule, similar to the shift from spoken to academic English.

dialogue.native: آیا واقعاً پیشرفت فناوری همیشه به نفع بشریت بوده است؟
dialogue.en: Has technological progress really always been to humanity's benefit?
This question does not have a simple answer.

dialogue.native: دقیقاً؛ باید هم فواید و هم پیامدهای آن را در نظر گرفت.
dialogue.en: Exactly; both its benefits and its consequences must be considered.

mastery-register.title: Mastery: Literary and Reflective Register
mastery-register.explanation: C2 is not about new grammar at all -- it's the ability to move fluidly between registers: everyday speech, formal argument, and the more elevated, literary register found in classical poetry, proverbs, and reflective essay writing, choosing the right one for the moment the way a native speaker instinctively does.
mastery-register.fact: Dari speakers, even in ordinary conversation, often reach for a line of Rumi, Hafez, or Bidel to make a point -- poetry is woven into everyday speech in a way that has no exact parallel in English conversation.

dialogue.native: این بیت از بیدل، همیشه مرا به فکر وامی‌دارد.
dialogue.en: This verse of Bidel always sets me thinking.

dialogue.native: بیدل زبانی دشوار اما عمیق دارد.
dialogue.en: Bidel has a difficult but profound language.

dialogue.native: دقیقاً به همین دلیل است که هر بار خواندنش، معنای نویی می‌یابم.
dialogue.en: That's exactly why every time I read him, I find a new meaning.
